question: Which statement correctly distinguishes `const int* p` from `int* const p`?

question: A class declares its single-argument constructor as `explicit`. What is the effect on this call: `void f(Meters m); f(5.0);` where Meters has an `explicit Meters(double)` constructor?

question: What happens if memory allocated with `new int[10]` is released with plain `delete arr;` instead of `delete[] arr;`?

question: Which statement about `enum class` (a scoped enum) is true, compared to a plain `enum`?

Its enumerators are scoped to the enum's name (e.g. Color::Red) and do NOT implicitly convert to int
It cannot have an explicit underlying type
It behaves identically to a plain enum in every way

question: Why does a well-designed `operator=` typically return `ClassType&` instead of `void`?

question: After `std::vector<int> v = {1,2,3}; auto it = v.begin(); v.push_back(4);` — is `it` still valid?

question: Which best describes the difference between a class template's full specialization and a partial specialization?

question: Which of the following is true about a `union` in C++?
options: All members occupy separate, non-overlapping memory, like a struct

All members share the same memory location; the union's size is at least the size of its largest member, and writing one member and reading a different one is generally undefined behavior (with narrow exceptions for "common initial sequence" layouts)
A union can have virtual member functions like a normal class

question: In C++, what is the result of comparing a signed int and an unsigned int directly, e.g. `int a = -1; unsigned int b = 1; if (a < b) ...`?

question: Which best describes `std::function<void()>` compared to a raw function pointer `void(*)()`?
options: std::function is a type-erased wrapper that can also hold lambdas with captures, functors, and bound member functions — not just plain function pointers — at the cost of some indirection/allocation overhead a raw pointer doesn't have
A raw function pointer can store lambda captures too, so there's no real difference
std::function only works with free functions, not lambdas
explanation: A plain function pointer can only point to a free function (or a captureless lambda, which is convertible to one) — it has no room to store captured state. std::function type-erases any callable (lambda with captures, functor, bound member function) behind a uniform interface, but that flexibility comes with extra overhead (often a heap allocation for larger captures, and an indirect/virtual-like call) that a hot path may want to avoid.

question: What is the average time complexity of `std::unordered_map::find`?

question: What is the time complexity of inserting at the FRONT of a std::vector via `insert(v.begin(), x)`?

O(1) always, since vector has spare capacity at the front

question: Two objects hold shared_ptrs to each other (A holds a shared_ptr<B>, B holds a shared_ptr<A>). What happens when all external references go out of scope?
options: Both are destroyed correctly, since shared_ptr always detects cycles
Neither is destroyed — a reference cycle keeps both reference counts above zero, causing a memory leak
Only A is destroyed, B leaks
explanation: std::shared_ptr uses plain reference counting, which cannot detect cycles. Each object's count never reaches zero because the other object still holds a reference to it — a classic reference-cycle leak. Fix: have one side hold a weak_ptr instead.

question: What is the time complexity of `std::vector::push_back` in the AMORTIZED sense, even though individual calls can trigger a full reallocation?

question: Which container is best suited for frequent insertions/removals at BOTH ends, while also supporting O(1) random access via operator[]?

question: After erasing an element from the MIDDLE of a std::list using `list.erase(it)`, what happens to OTHER iterators pointing to different, still-present elements of the list?
options: All iterators into the list are invalidated
Only the erased element's own iterator is invalidated; all other iterators/references/pointers remain valid
Only iterators before the erased element are invalidated
std::list does not support erase on middle elements
explanation: std::list is a node-based container (doubly linked list); erasing a node only invalidates iterators/references to THAT node. This is a key advantage over std::vector, where erasing/inserting can invalidate many or all iterators.

question: What does `std::make_shared<T>(args...)` do differently from `std::shared_ptr<T>(new T(args...))`?
options: Nothing — they are functionally and performance-wise identical
make_shared performs a single combined heap allocation for both the control block and the object, instead of two separate allocations — better for performance and exception safety
make_shared cannot be used with custom deleters, but the other form can — that's the only difference
make_shared creates a weak_ptr instead of a shared_ptr
explanation: `shared_ptr<T>(new T(...))` allocates T and its control block (ref counts) separately — two allocations. `make_shared<T>(...)` allocates both together in one block, reducing allocation overhead and improving cache locality — the standard recommendation is to prefer make_shared unless you need a custom deleter or already have a raw pointer.

question: What is a downside of `std::make_shared` regarding memory reclamation, compared to separate allocation?
options: It has no downsides at all

Because the object and control block share one allocation, the memory for the object itself can't be freed until ALL weak_ptrs referencing it are also gone (not just when the last shared_ptr is destroyed)
It cannot be used with polymorphic types
It always leaks memory if an exception is thrown
explanation: With combined allocation, the block backing both the object and control block can only be freed once the control block's weak-reference count also hits zero — so a lingering weak_ptr can keep the (already-destroyed) object's memory allocated slightly longer than it would with separate allocations.

question: What is the key difference between `std::map` and `std::unordered_map` in terms of iteration order?
options: Both iterate in sorted key order
std::map iterates in sorted key order (typically a red-black tree); std::unordered_map's iteration order is unspecified and depends on the hash function/bucket layout
explanation: std::map is typically implemented as a balanced binary search tree (red-black tree), so iterating it visits keys in sorted order. std::unordered_map is hash-table based and gives no ordering guarantee at all.

question: Why should a destructor almost never throw an exception in C++?
options: Destructors are physically incapable of executing throw statements

If a destructor throws WHILE another exception is already propagating (e.g., during stack unwinding), std::terminate is called immediately, crashing the program — and destructors are implicitly `noexcept` by default since C++11, so an escaping exception there calls terminate even in the ordinary case
Throwing from a destructor is fine as long as it's caught inside the same destructor
Destructors run before the object's memory exists, so exceptions can't propagate
explanation: Special member functions like destructors are noexcept by default in C++11+. If an exception tries to escape a destructor, std::terminate is called — this is especially dangerous during stack unwinding from another exception, where two simultaneously-propagating exceptions is explicitly documented to call std::terminate.

question: Which STL algorithm/approach correctly removes all elements equal to a value from a std::vector while keeping it a vector (not just "marking" them)?
options: v.erase(std::remove(v.begin(), v.end(), value), v.end());  (the erase-remove idiom)
std::erase_all(v, value); — the only correct C++11 method
Simply calling std::remove(v.begin(), v.end(), value) is sufficient on its own
explanation: std::remove doesn't actually shrink the container — it moves the "kept" elements to the front and returns an iterator to the new logical end, leaving unspecified values in the remaining tail slots. You must follow it with `erase(...)` to actually shrink the vector — this is the classic "erase-remove idiom". (Since C++20, `std::erase(v, value)` does both steps for you.)

question: What does `std::vector<int> v; v.reserve(100);` do?
options: Immediately creates 100 default-constructed int elements (size() becomes 100)
Pre-allocates capacity for at least 100 elements without changing size() — future push_backs up to that count won't trigger reallocation
Limits the vector to a maximum of 100 elements forever

explanation: reserve(n) allocates capacity without adding elements — size() stays 0, but capacity() becomes at least 100, so up to 100 subsequent push_backs won't reallocate (and won't invalidate iterators from reallocation). Use resize() if you want size() itself to grow with default-constructed elements.

question: What is the primary reason `std::map` and `std::set` typically have worse cache performance than `std::vector` for sequential scans, despite `std::map`'s O(log n) lookup being asymptotically fast?
options: std::map always stores data on a different CPU core
std::map's nodes are individually heap-allocated and scattered in memory, so traversal jumps between non-contiguous cache lines, unlike a vector's contiguous, cache-friendly layout
std::map uses more bytes per key than std::vector, which is the only reason for the slowdown
There is no real performance difference in practice
explanation: Tree-based containers allocate each node separately, so nodes are scattered across memory (poor spatial locality) and traversal causes many cache misses and pointer chases. A sorted std::vector (with binary search) or a flat_map-style structure is often faster in practice for read-heavy workloads specifically because of this cache-locality advantage, despite big-O being the same or worse.

question: What is the key behavioral difference between `std::vector::at(i)` and `std::vector::operator[](i)` for an out-of-range index?
options: at(i) throws std::out_of_range for an invalid index; operator[] performs no bounds checking and invokes undefined behavior on an invalid index
operator[] throws; at() is undefined behavior
Both always return a default-constructed value on invalid index
explanation: at() is the bounds-checked accessor (a small runtime cost, but safe). operator[] is unchecked for performance — indexing out of bounds is undefined behavior, which is why hot-path code often uses operator[] deliberately (after validating bounds itself) while at() is preferred where safety matters more than the last bit of speed.

question: Which of these is a correct, complete implementation pattern for a basic reference-counted smart pointer's copy constructor?

explanation: A reference-counted (shared_ptr-style) copy constructor must increment the shared refcount after copying the pointer, so the destructor logic (which decrements and frees at zero) correctly accounts for the new copy sharing ownership.

question: What is the effect of calling `.clear()` on a std::vector<int>?
options: Destroys all elements and sets size() to 0, but typically leaves capacity() unchanged (does not necessarily free the underlying buffer)
Frees all memory immediately, setting both size() and capacity() to 0
Sets every element to 0 without changing size()
Is equivalent to calling the destructor of the vector object itself
explanation: clear() destroys the contained elements and sets size() to 0, but the standard does not require it to release the allocated storage — capacity() commonly stays the same, which is useful if you plan to refill the vector without reallocating. Use the "swap with an empty temporary" trick (or shrink_to_fit()) to actually release capacity.

question: What does `std::move(x)` actually DO to `x` at the moment it's called?
options: It immediately transfers x's resources to wherever the result is used
Nothing by itself — it's just a cast to an rvalue reference (T&&); the actual "move" only happens if that rvalue reference is then bound to a move constructor/move-assignment operator
It makes x thread-safe for the rest of the program
explanation: std::move performs no operation on its own — it's purely a static_cast to T&&, signaling "this may be moved from." Whether a move actually happens (and what state x is left in) depends entirely on what overload subsequently receives that rvalue reference.

question: What state is an object left in after being moved from (e.g., after `T b = std::move(a);` where T has a typical move constructor)?
options: a is guaranteed to be exactly default-constructed
a is guaranteed to be destroyed immediately
a is left in a "valid but unspecified" state — it's safe to destroy or reassign, but its specific value shouldn't be relied upon unless the type explicitly documents otherwise
a still holds a full independent copy of its original value
explanation: The standard's general guarantee for moved-from objects of standard library types is "valid but unspecified state" — you can still safely call operations like assignment or destruction on it, but should not assume anything about its contents (e.g., a moved-from vector might be empty, or might not be — that detail is implementation-specific).

question: Which of the following is the most idiomatic way to remove duplicate elements from an already-SORTED std::vector<int>?
options: There is no STL support for this; you must write a manual loop
explanation: std::unique reorders consecutive duplicate elements to the end (like remove, it doesn't resize the container) and returns an iterator to the new logical end; erase() then trims the container — the same erase-X idiom pattern as remove. (Note: unique() only removes CONSECUTIVE duplicates, which is why the vector must be sorted first for this to remove ALL duplicates.)

question: What is the amortized time complexity of `std::unordered_map::insert` when the load factor forces a rehash?
options: Always O(1), rehashing has no cost
A single insert triggering rehash is O(n) (every existing element must be re-hashed into new buckets), but amortized over many inserts it remains O(1) — analogous to vector's geometric growth
O(n^2) in the worst case for any insert
explanation: Just like std::vector's capacity growth, unordered_map grows its bucket array geometrically when the load factor threshold is exceeded, re-hashing all elements — an O(n) operation. But because this happens exponentially less often as the container grows, the AMORTIZED cost per insert remains O(1).

question: Why might a custom memory pool/arena allocator be used instead of the default allocator (`operator new`) for objects on a hot trading path?
options: Custom allocators are always required by the C++ standard for STL containers

The general-purpose heap allocator involves locking, bookkeeping, and unpredictable latency (and potential syscalls like mmap/brk); a pre-sized arena can hand out fixed-size chunks in O(1), predictable time with no lock contention
Custom allocators automatically make code thread-safe
There is no performance benefit; it's purely a stylistic choice
explanation: General-purpose allocators are optimized for a wide variety of allocation patterns and often involve internal locks and bookkeeping overhead, with tail latencies that are hard to bound. In HFT, a pre-allocated arena/pool sized for known object counts avoids calling into the general allocator (and its jitter) entirely during the hot path.

question: What does the following print?
explanation: `b` receives the moved-from content of `a` via the move constructor — b now holds "hello" with size 5. (It's `a`, not `b`, whose state afterward is valid-but-unspecified — this question is about b, the destination of the move.)

question: Which container should you reach for when you need a FIFO queue with O(1) push at the back and O(1) pop at the front, and don't need random access?
options: std::queue (typically implemented as an adapter over std::deque)
explanation: std::queue is a container adapter (default underlying container: std::deque) purpose-built for FIFO push_back/pop_front semantics, both O(1) amortized.

question: What's the effect of NOT declaring a base class's destructor `virtual` when the class is intended to be used polymorphically (deleted through base pointers)?
options: No effect; C++ always calls the most-derived destructor regardless
`delete basePtr;` only invokes the base class's destructor, skipping any derived-class cleanup (member destructors, freed resources) — undefined behavior, commonly manifesting as a resource leak
Only the derived destructor runs, skipping the base
explanation: Without a virtual destructor, deleting through a base pointer statically resolves to the base's destructor only — derived members and any resources they own never get cleaned up. This is one of the most frequently tested "what's wrong with this class hierarchy" interview questions.

question: What is "iterator invalidation" a concern for specifically with `std::unordered_map`, even without any erase/insert?
options: Inserting an element that triggers a REHASH invalidates ALL iterators (though references/pointers to existing elements remain valid across a rehash, unlike vector)
Simply reading a value invalidates its iterator
unordered_map iterators are permanently valid for the container's whole lifetime no matter what
explanation: For std::unordered_map, a rehash (triggered by insertion crossing the load-factor threshold) invalidates all iterators, but — unlike vector — references and pointers to the actual stored elements remain valid across a rehash, since elements aren't moved/copied, only re-bucketed.

question: What does `std::array<int, 5>` provide that a raw C-style array `int[5]` does not?
options: A fixed-size container with STL-compatible interface (size(), begin()/end(), works with algorithms), value semantics (safely copyable, unlike array-to-pointer decay), and bounds-checked access via .at() — all with zero overhead versus a raw array
explanation: std::array wraps a fixed-size raw array in a proper STL-container interface — no decay-to-pointer surprises, works with range-based for and STL algorithms, supports `.at()` for bounds-checked access — all while keeping the same stack storage and zero runtime overhead as a plain C array.

question: Two threads increment a shared, plain (non-atomic) `int counter` a million times each with `counter++`, with no synchronization. What is the most accurate description of the result?
options: This is a data race — undefined behavior; the final value is unpredictable and typically less than 2,000,000 due to lost updates
The program is guaranteed to crash
explanation: `counter++` is a read-modify-write that is NOT atomic for a plain int. Concurrent unsynchronized reads/writes to the same non-atomic variable from multiple threads (with at least one write) is a data race, which is undefined behavior by the C++ memory model — in practice this usually manifests as lost updates (final value less than 2,000,000), but the standard makes no guarantee at all.

question: What is the ABA problem in lock-free programming?
options: A thread reads value A, another thread changes it to B and back to A before the first thread's compare-and-swap runs — the CAS succeeds thinking nothing changed, even though the underlying state (e.g., freed/reallocated memory) may have changed in between
A occurs before B in alphabetical order, causing sort instability
Two threads both named 'A' and 'B' deadlock
A CPU cache issue unrelated to concurrency
explanation: ABA is a classic lock-free hazard: a compare-and-swap only checks the CURRENT value equals the expected value, not whether the value changed in between reads. If a pointer/value goes A->B->A, a naive CAS can't tell the difference from "never changed," which is dangerous if B's transition involved freeing/reusing memory. Fixes include tagged pointers (a version counter alongside the value) or hazard pointers.

question: Which best describes the difference between a mutex and a spinlock?
options: They are exactly the same thing under different names

A mutex typically puts a blocked thread to sleep (yielding the CPU, involving an OS context switch) if the lock is held; a spinlock busy-waits (polling in a tight loop) instead — spinlocks avoid context-switch cost for very short critical sections but waste CPU while waiting
A spinlock is always slower than a mutex in every scenario
A mutex can be used across process boundaries, but a spinlock never can
explanation: Mutexes generally involve the OS scheduler (blocking, context switch) — good when waits are longer or unpredictable. Spinlocks poll on the CPU without yielding — good ONLY for very short critical sections where the cost of a context switch would exceed the wait itself, which is why they show up in low-latency code, but they waste CPU cycles (and can be actively harmful under CPU oversubscription) otherwise.

question: In `std::atomic`, what does `memory_order_relaxed` guarantee?
options: Full sequential consistency across all threads
Only atomicity of the individual operation itself — no ordering guarantee relative to other memory operations in the same thread or other threads
That the operation will never be reordered by the compiler
That the operation acquires a lock internally
explanation: memory_order_relaxed is the weakest ordering: it guarantees the operation itself is atomic (no torn reads/writes), but places no constraint on how it can be reordered relative to other memory operations — useful for things like independent counters where you only need atomicity, not cross-thread visibility ordering.

question: What does the acquire/release pairing on `std::atomic<bool> ready` typically guarantee in this pattern?
options: Nothing extra beyond relaxed ordering — data could still be seen as uninitialized in Thread 2

Once Thread 2 observes ready==true via the acquire load, it is guaranteed to also see the write to `data` that happened-before the release store — establishing safe cross-thread visibility without a full mutex
It guarantees data is written atomically, but not that it's visible to Thread 2
It only works if both threads run on the same CPU core
explanation: This is the canonical release/acquire synchronization pattern: a release store makes all prior writes in that thread visible to any thread that acquire-loads the same atomic and observes the new value — establishing a happens-before relationship without needing a full mutex or seq_cst fence.

question: What is "false sharing"?
options: A security vulnerability caused by sharing a file across permission boundaries

Two threads write to different variables that happen to reside on the same CPU cache line, causing the cache-coherence protocol to repeatedly invalidate/reload that line between cores — a performance problem, not a correctness one
When a shared_ptr's reference count is shared incorrectly between threads
A compiler bug that shares incorrect values between variables
explanation: False sharing happens purely at the hardware cache level: even though the two threads' variables are logically independent, they sit on the same 64-byte cache line, so writes by either thread cause expensive cache-coherence traffic (invalidations) on the other core — hurting performance without causing any actual logical data race.

question: Which of these is a valid, common fix for false sharing between two hot per-thread counters in a struct?
options: Pad/align each field to its own cache line, e.g. `alignas(64) std::atomic<long> a; alignas(64) std::atomic<long> b;`
Combine a and b into a single atomic<long> to save memory
Move both fields into thread_local storage without any other change
explanation: Aligning each hot, independently-written field to its own cache line (commonly 64 bytes via `alignas(64)`) ensures the two counters never share a cache line, eliminating the false-sharing cross-core invalidation traffic — at the cost of extra memory (padding).

question: What is a deadlock, and which of the following four conditions is NOT one of the classic necessary conditions for deadlock (Coffman conditions)?
options: Mutual exclusion (a resource can only be held by one thread at a time)
Hold and wait (a thread holds a resource while waiting for another)
Preemption allowed (the OS can forcibly take a resource away from a thread at any time)
Circular wait (a cycle of threads each waiting on a resource held by the next)
explanation: The Coffman conditions for deadlock are: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, NO preemption (resources cannot be forcibly taken away), and circular wait. "Preemption allowed" is the opposite of the actual condition — deadlock requires that preemption is NOT possible.

question: Two threads each try to lock two mutexes in opposite order: Thread 1 locks A then B; Thread 2 locks B then A. What is the risk?
options: No risk — mutexes always grant access in request order
Classic deadlock: Thread 1 holds A waiting for B, Thread 2 holds B waiting for A, and neither can proceed
This always causes a crash immediately, not a hang
This pattern is safe as long as both mutexes are the same type
explanation: Inconsistent lock ordering across threads is one of the most common real deadlock causes. The standard fix is to always acquire multiple locks in a single, globally consistent order (or use std::lock()/std::scoped_lock with multiple mutexes, which is deadlock-avoiding by internally imposing a consistent acquisition strategy).

question: What does `std::lock_guard` provide that manually calling `mutex.lock()` / `mutex.unlock()` does not?
options: RAII-based automatic unlocking — the mutex is released when the lock_guard goes out of scope, including via early return or an exception, preventing forgotten/missed unlocks
The ability to lock multiple mutexes atomically
Support for recursive locking by the same thread
explanation: lock_guard is a thin RAII wrapper: it locks the mutex in its constructor and unlocks it in its destructor. This guarantees the mutex is released even if an exception is thrown or the function returns early — eliminating a whole class of "forgot to unlock" bugs from manual lock/unlock calls.

question: What does a condition variable's `wait()` call typically need to guard against, requiring it to be called in a loop checking a predicate rather than a single `if`?
code:
std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(m);
while (!ready) { cv.wait(lk); }
options: Deadlock — wait() can never be called more than once
Spurious wakeups — the OS/implementation is permitted to wake a waiting thread even when no one explicitly notified it, so the condition must be re-checked after every wakeup
Memory leaks in the condition variable object
Nothing — a single `if` check is always sufficient
explanation: POSIX condition variables (and std::condition_variable) are explicitly allowed to wake a waiter spuriously, with no corresponding notify. The correct pattern always re-checks the actual predicate in a loop (or uses the predicate-overload of wait()) rather than assuming a single wakeup means the condition is now true.

question: What distinguishes a "lock-free" algorithm from a "wait-free" one?
options: Lock-free guarantees that SOME thread among all contending threads makes progress in a bounded number of steps (no global blocking, though an individual thread could theoretically be starved); wait-free guarantees EVERY thread makes progress in a bounded number of steps, regardless of what other threads do
Wait-free is a weaker guarantee than lock-free
Lock-free means no atomics are used at all
explanation: Lock-free is a system-wide progress guarantee (at least one thread always advances); wait-free is a much stronger, per-thread guarantee (every individual thread advances in bounded time, even under adversarial scheduling). Wait-free algorithms are harder to design and less common in practice; most "lock-free" data structures used in industry are lock-free, not wait-free.

question: Why is a single-producer single-consumer (SPSC) lock-free ring buffer often implemented WITHOUT any atomic read-modify-write (CAS) operations at all, just plain atomic loads/stores of the head/tail indices?
options: It's not actually possible to avoid CAS in an SPSC queue

With exactly one producer and one consumer, there's never contention on WHO gets to write a given index — only the producer ever writes the tail (write) index and only the consumer ever writes the head (read) index, so simple atomic loads/stores with acquire/release ordering are sufficient to synchronize visibility
CAS is always faster, so this is purely a stylistic/legacy choice
SPSC queues cannot use atomics of any kind
explanation: SPSC is a special, easier case: since only one thread ever produces (advances the write index) and only one ever consumes (advances the read index), there's no race on who updates which index — you only need release/acquire ordering to make each side's writes visible to the other, not a full compare-and-swap loop as in the general multi-producer/multi-consumer case.

question: What is the primary purpose of a memory fence / barrier instruction (e.g. issued by std::atomic_thread_fence)?
options: To physically stop the CPU clock temporarily
To prevent the CPU and/or compiler from reordering memory operations across the fence, establishing an ordering guarantee between operations before and after it
To allocate memory for atomic variables
To lock a mutex without blocking
explanation: Both compilers and out-of-order CPUs are free to reorder memory operations as long as single-threaded observable behavior is unchanged — which can break multithreaded assumptions. A memory fence constrains this reordering across the fence point, which is how acquire/release semantics and other ordering guarantees are actually implemented at the hardware/compiler level.

question: Why can a `std::mutex` be a poor choice on an ultra-low-latency hot path even when contention is rare?
options: std::mutex always spins forever, wasting CPU

Even an uncontended lock/unlock has non-trivial and somewhat unpredictable latency (it may involve a syscall/futex path in the contended case, and the mutex itself isn't guaranteed lock-free), which conflicts with the goal of tight, predictable tail latency
std::mutex cannot be used with more than 2 threads
std::mutex requires heap allocation on every lock() call
explanation: While a fast-path uncontended std::mutex lock is cheap on modern implementations, the worst case (contention triggering a futex/syscall wait) has much higher and less predictable latency — which is exactly what latency-sensitive trading code tries to avoid via lock-free structures or careful lock-free designs on the hottest paths.

question: What does `compare_exchange_weak` do differently from `compare_exchange_strong` on `std::atomic<T>`?
options: weak always succeeds; strong can fail

weak may fail spuriously (return false even though the current value did equal the expected value), typically due to platform-specific load-linked/store-conditional instructions — it's meant to be used in a retry loop, and can be more efficient on such platforms; strong never fails spuriously
strong is only available on x86, weak only on ARM
They are identical in the C++ standard
explanation: On platforms using LL/SC (load-linked/store-conditional) primitives (common on ARM/POWER), compare_exchange_weak can fail spuriously due to intervening events unrelated to the actual value — this is acceptable because it's meant to be called in a loop anyway (e.g. classic CAS-retry patterns), and avoiding the strong version's internal retry-on-spurious-failure loop can be more efficient there.

question: In a multi-producer, single-consumer (MPSC) lock-free queue, why do producers typically need an atomic compare-and-swap (or fetch-and-add) on the shared tail index, while an SPSC queue does not?
options: MPSC queues never need atomics either

With multiple producers, more than one thread can attempt to claim the same slot/advance the same tail index concurrently — a CAS loop (or atomic fetch-and-add) is needed to safely resolve which producer "wins" each slot, a race that simply doesn't exist with only one producer
CAS is required only for the consumer side, never the producer side
Because MPSC queues are always implemented with mutexes instead
explanation: The defining difference from SPSC is contention on the producer side: multiple threads racing to claim the next write slot need an atomic read-modify-write (CAS retry loop or fetch_add) to safely coordinate who gets which index, since a plain non-atomic increment could let two producers claim the same slot.

question: What does `std::atomic<T>::is_lock_free()` tell you?
options: Whether the atomic variable is currently locked by another thread

Whether operations on this atomic type are implemented WITHOUT an internal mutex/lock on the current platform — for some types/platforms (e.g. atomics on types larger than the machine's native word size), the implementation may fall back to using an internal lock, making it technically atomic but not truly lock-free
Whether the variable can be safely read without any synchronization at all
Whether the compiler optimized away the atomic entirely
explanation: std::atomic guarantees ATOMICITY of operations, but not necessarily a LOCK-FREE implementation — for types that don't map cleanly onto a hardware atomic instruction (e.g. a large struct), the standard library may implement the atomic using an internal mutex. is_lock_free() lets you check which case you're in at runtime (it's often, but not always, a compile-time constant).

question: Which statement about thread priorities and CPU pinning (affinity) is most relevant to low-latency trading systems?
options: They are irrelevant since modern OS schedulers are always optimal

Pinning latency-critical threads to dedicated, isolated CPU cores (and raising their scheduling priority) reduces jitter from context switches, cache eviction by other processes, and cross-core migration — a common technique to tighten tail latency
CPU pinning is illegal in most operating systems
Thread priority has no effect on scheduling in Linux
explanation: Letting the OS scheduler freely migrate a hot thread between cores (losing warm cache state) or preempt it for unrelated work introduces latency jitter. Pinning critical threads to isolated cores (e.g., via CPU affinity and kernel isolcpus) and using real-time scheduling policies is a standard low-latency systems technique to get more predictable, lower tail latency.

question: What triggers a context switch on a typical operating system?
options: Only when a process explicitly calls exit()

The scheduler suspending the currently running thread/process (saving its registers/state) and resuming another — triggered by a timer interrupt (time slice expiry), a higher-priority task becoming ready, or the current task blocking (e.g. on I/O or a lock)
Only hardware resets can cause a context switch
Context switches only happen once per second on a fixed timer
explanation: A context switch happens whenever the CPU is reassigned from one thread/process to another — due to time-slice expiry (preemption), the running task blocking on I/O or a synchronization primitive, or a higher-priority task preempting it. Each switch has real cost (saving/restoring registers, and often flushing/reloading cache and TLB state), which is why minimizing unnecessary context switches matters for latency-sensitive code.

question: What is virtual memory, and what problem does it primarily solve?
options: A way to make RAM run faster via caching

An abstraction giving each process its own private, contiguous address space, backed by a mapping (page table) to physical memory (or disk) managed by the OS/MMU — providing process isolation, allowing programs larger than physical RAM, and simplifying memory management
A feature only used by virtual machines, not regular processes
A type of memory that doesn't actually exist physically anywhere
explanation: Virtual memory lets each process address memory as if it had its own full, contiguous space, translated to physical addresses by the MMU via page tables. This provides isolation between processes, allows overcommitting physical RAM (paging to disk), and lets the OS relocate physical pages transparently.

question: What is a page fault?
options: A hardware error that always crashes the program

A trap triggered when a process accesses a virtual memory page that isn't currently mapped to physical memory (e.g. it's been swapped out, or is being loaded lazily) — the OS handles it by loading the page (or, for an invalid access, delivering a segmentation fault)
A syntax error caught by the compiler
An error only possible in embedded systems without an MMU
explanation: A page fault occurs whenever the MMU can't satisfy a virtual-to-physical address translation from the current page table (page not present, or a protection violation). A "minor" fault (e.g., lazily allocated/demand-paged memory) is resolved by the OS mapping in a page; a fault on a genuinely invalid address results in a segmentation fault delivered to the process.

question: Why do latency-sensitive applications sometimes use "huge pages" (e.g. 2MB pages instead of the standard 4KB)?
options: Huge pages make RAM physically larger

Fewer, larger pages mean fewer entries are needed to map the same amount of memory, reducing TLB (translation lookaside buffer) misses — a TLB miss requires a page-table walk, which is relatively slow and adds latency jitter on memory-heavy hot paths
Huge pages are required for any multithreaded program
Huge pages eliminate the need for virtual memory entirely
explanation: The TLB caches a limited number of virtual-to-physical page translations. With standard 4KB pages, a large working set needs many TLB entries and causes frequent misses (each requiring a slower page-table walk). Using 2MB or 1GB huge pages covers the same memory with far fewer entries, improving TLB hit rate and reducing latency variance — a known low-latency systems tuning technique.

question: What is the key difference in guarantees between TCP and UDP?
options: They are functionally identical, just different port ranges

TCP is connection-oriented and guarantees reliable, ordered, error-checked delivery with flow/congestion control (at the cost of overhead/latency); UDP is connectionless and provides no delivery/ordering guarantees, but with much lower overhead and more predictable per-packet latency
UDP guarantees delivery order, TCP does not
TCP is always faster than UDP in every scenario
explanation: TCP's reliability machinery (acknowledgements, retransmission, ordering, congestion control) adds overhead and can introduce latency spikes (e.g., waiting for a retransmit). UDP simply fires packets with no such guarantees — which is exactly why market-data multicast feeds in HFT use UDP: an occasional dropped packet is preferable to TCP's head-of-line blocking and retransmission delay.

question: Why do market-data distribution systems commonly use UDP MULTICAST rather than TCP unicast connections to each subscriber?
options: Multicast is required by financial regulation

With multicast, the sender transmits each packet once and the network (switches/routers) replicates it to all subscribed receivers, instead of the sender needing a separate TCP connection and separate copy of each message per subscriber — this scales far better to many simultaneous consumers of the same feed
TCP cannot be used for financial data for security reasons
explanation: Multicast offloads the fan-out/replication work to the network infrastructure rather than the sender, so publishing to 1 subscriber or 10,000 costs the sender roughly the same — critical for exchanges and market-data vendors broadcasting the same feed to many consumers simultaneously.

question: What does "kernel bypass" networking (e.g. via DPDK or Solarflare OpenOnload) achieve, and why?
options: It bypasses network hardware entirely, using only software

It lets an application send/receive network packets directly from/to the NIC in userspace, skipping the kernel's network stack (socket buffers, interrupts, context switches into kernel mode) — removing a major source of latency and jitter for the highest-performance trading systems
It's a way to bypass firewall rules
It only works for UDP, never for any other protocol
explanation: The traditional kernel networking path involves interrupts, context switches, and copies through kernel buffers — each adding latency and, more importantly, jitter (unpredictability). Kernel-bypass frameworks map the NIC's queues directly into a userspace process (often combined with polling instead of interrupts) so packets can be processed with far lower and more consistent latency.

question: In the TCP three-way handshake, what is the correct sequence?
explanation: The client sends SYN (synchronize) to initiate; the server responds SYN-ACK (acknowledging the client's SYN and sending its own SYN); the client responds with a final ACK, completing the connection setup before any data is exchanged.

question: What does the `TCP_NODELAY` socket option do, and why does latency-sensitive trading software often set it?
options: It makes the socket use UDP instead of TCP

It disables Nagle's algorithm, which by default buffers small outgoing packets to combine them into fewer, larger packets — Nagle's algorithm trades latency for network efficiency, which is the wrong tradeoff for small, latency-critical messages sent one at a time
It increases the socket's receive buffer size
It forces the connection to close immediately after each send
explanation: Nagle's algorithm delays sending small packets to batch them, reducing the NUMBER of packets at the cost of added latency — great for bulk/interactive traffic, bad for latency-sensitive small messages (like order/quote messages) that need to go out immediately. TCP_NODELAY disables that buffering.

question: Which OSI layer does a network switch primarily operate at (in its basic, non-"layer 3 switch" form), and which does a router operate at?
options: Switch: Layer 2 (Data Link, using MAC addresses); Router: Layer 3 (Network, using IP addresses)
explanation: A basic switch forwards frames within a local network based on MAC addresses (Layer 2). A router forwards packets BETWEEN different networks based on IP addresses (Layer 3), making routing decisions using routing tables.

question: What is a CPU cache line, and why does its size (commonly 64 bytes) matter for performance-sensitive code?
options: It's the maximum instruction length the CPU can execute

It's the smallest unit of data transferred between main memory and the CPU cache; accessing ANY byte within a line pulls the WHOLE line into cache, so laying out frequently-accessed data to fit within (and align to) cache lines improves spatial locality, while unrelated hot variables sharing a line can cause false sharing between cores
It refers to the physical wiring length inside the CPU die
It only matters for GPU programming, not CPU
explanation: Caches operate on fixed-size lines, not individual bytes. Understanding this drives real design decisions: packing hot data together to maximize useful bytes per cache line (good locality) versus separating independently-modified hot variables onto different lines (avoiding false sharing).

question: What is branch prediction, and why can a MISPREDICTED branch be costly on modern CPUs?
options: Branch prediction is a compiler-only optimization with no CPU involvement

Modern CPUs speculatively execute instructions ALONG the predicted path of a conditional branch before the condition is actually known, to keep a deep pipeline full; if the prediction is wrong, all that speculative work must be discarded and the pipeline refilled from the correct path — a real, measurable latency penalty (often 10-20+ cycles)
Branches are always resolved instantly with no cost either way
Branch prediction only affects floating-point instructions
explanation: CPUs pipeline many instructions in flight and predict which way a branch will go to avoid stalling. A misprediction means the speculatively-executed instructions were wasted work and must be flushed, then the correct path fetched — a pipeline-flush penalty that's a common target of performance-sensitive code (e.g., writing branch-free / data-oriented code, or structuring hot loops to be predictable).

question: What does "out-of-order execution" mean in a modern CPU, and what has to be true for the program to still behave correctly?
options: Instructions are executed in a random order every run, with no consistency guarantees for the program

The CPU can execute instructions in a different order than they appear in the program (as their operands become ready) to keep execution units busy, but it must guarantee results are COMMITTED (retired) in a way that preserves the illusion of in-order, single-threaded execution to the program itself
It refers only to disk I/O ordering, not instruction execution
It means the compiler reorders source code randomly before compiling
explanation: Out-of-order execution lets independent instructions run as soon as their inputs are ready rather than strictly in program order, hiding latency (e.g., of a cache miss) by doing other useful work meanwhile. The CPU's retirement stage ensures results still appear to commit in original program order for single-threaded correctness — the reordering is invisible to correctly-written single-threaded code, but becomes visible (and requires explicit memory ordering/fences) across threads.

question: What is NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access), and why does it matter for a multi-socket server running latency-sensitive software?
options: NUMA is a caching algorithm used only in GPUs

In a multi-socket system, each CPU socket has its own "local" memory bank; accessing memory attached to a DIFFERENT socket ("remote" memory) takes measurably longer than accessing local memory — so pinning a thread and its data to the same NUMA node avoids extra cross-socket memory latency
NUMA means all memory access times are always exactly uniform
NUMA only affects storage devices, not RAM
explanation: On NUMA systems, memory is physically attached to specific CPU sockets. A thread on socket 0 accessing memory allocated on socket 1's bank pays extra latency traversing the inter-socket interconnect. Low-latency systems explicitly pin threads and allocate their working memory on the same NUMA node to avoid this penalty.

question: What is the purpose of a Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB)?
options: It buffers network packets awaiting translation between protocols

It's a small, fast cache inside the CPU that stores recent virtual-to-physical address translations, avoiding the cost of a full page-table walk on every memory access — a TLB miss requires walking the (potentially multi-level) page table, which is comparatively slow
It translates machine code between different CPU architectures at runtime
It converts floating-point numbers between formats
explanation: Every memory access needs a virtual-to-physical translation. Walking the page table structure for every single access would be far too slow, so the TLB caches recent translations — a TLB miss (forcing a page-table walk) is a real, measurable latency cost, which is part of why huge pages (fewer, larger mappings) help latency-sensitive workloads.

question: What does `mmap`-ing a file into a process's address space allow, compared to reading it with regular `read()` calls?
options: mmap always reads the whole file into RAM immediately, unlike read()

mmap maps the file's contents directly into the process's virtual address space, letting the process access file data via normal memory reads/writes (with the kernel lazily paging in data on demand) instead of copying data through an explicit read() buffer — useful for large files and for sharing memory between processes
mmap can only be used for network sockets, not files
mmap disables all caching for the file
explanation: mmap avoids an explicit copy into a userspace buffer (the kernel maps pages directly, faulting them in on first access) and lets a file be accessed with ordinary pointer/array semantics — useful for large or randomly-accessed files, and it's also the mechanism behind shared memory between processes when mapping the same underlying object.

question: What is the difference between DNS's role and HTTP's role in loading a web page?
options: DNS translates a human-readable domain name into an IP address (a naming/lookup service); HTTP is the application-layer protocol used to actually request and transfer the page's content once the IP address is known
HTTP resolves domain names; DNS transfers the actual page content
Neither is involved in loading a web page
explanation: DNS resolution happens first, translating e.g. "example.com" into an IP address. Only after that does the browser open a TCP connection to that IP and issue an HTTP request to actually retrieve the page content.

question: What is a race condition, as distinguished from a data race?
options: They are exactly the same concept with different names

A data race is a specific technical condition (concurrent unsynchronized access to the same memory, at least one write) that is undefined behavior in C++; a race condition is the broader concept of a program's correctness depending on the unpredictable relative TIMING/ordering of events — a program can have a race condition (a logic bug from bad interleaving) even with properly synchronized (non-data-racing) accesses
Data races only happen in single-threaded programs
Race conditions can only occur in networked systems, never in local multithreaded code
explanation: A data race is specifically about unsynchronized concurrent memory access (a C++ standard term with UB consequences). A race condition is the more general software-engineering concept: a bug where correctness depends on timing/interleaving, which can occur even with properly locked/synchronized code if the LOGIC of what's synchronized is wrong (e.g., a correctly-locked check-then-act sequence that's still logically racy across two separate critical sections).

question: What is copy-on-write (COW), commonly used when a process calls `fork()`?
options: The child process immediately gets a full, separate physical copy of all the parent's memory

Parent and child initially SHARE the same physical memory pages (marked read-only); only when either process writes to a shared page does the kernel copy that specific page, giving the writer its own private copy — deferring (and often entirely avoiding) the cost of copying memory that's never modified
COW means the child process can never write to any memory
COW only applies to files on disk, not process memory
explanation: fork() would be prohibitively expensive if it always deep-copied a process's entire address space immediately. Copy-on-write defers actual copying until a write actually happens to a shared page, which is a major reason fork() is practically usable despite processes potentially having large address spaces.

question: Which scheduling approach is generally preferred for a latency-critical trading thread that must run with minimal, predictable delay, versus the default time-sharing scheduler most processes use?
options: The default best-effort scheduler is always sufficient for any workload

A real-time scheduling policy (e.g. Linux's SCHED_FIFO or SCHED_RR) combined with CPU isolation/pinning, so the thread preempts normal time-shared processes and isn't subject to the same fairness-driven delays as ordinary tasks
Lowering the thread's priority so it never runs, ensuring no interference
Real-time scheduling is illegal to use outside embedded systems
explanation: The default Completely Fair Scheduler on Linux optimizes for overall throughput/fairness across many processes, which can introduce scheduling latency for any individual thread. Real-time policies (SCHED_FIFO/SCHED_RR) let a designated thread preempt normal tasks and run with much more predictable, lower latency — commonly combined with isolating dedicated CPU cores for these threads.

question: What is the Banker's Algorithm used for?
options: Calculating interest rates for a trading system

A deadlock AVOIDANCE algorithm: given advance knowledge of each process's maximum possible resource needs, it only grants a resource request if doing so leaves the system in a "safe state" (a state from which all processes can still eventually finish) — preventing deadlock before it happens rather than detecting/recovering from it after
A CPU scheduling algorithm for I/O-bound processes
explanation: The Banker's Algorithm is a classic OS textbook deadlock-avoidance technique: it simulates whether granting a resource request could ever lead to an unsafe state (one where some process's future needs cannot be satisfied) and denies requests that would create that risk.

question: What does the Least Recently Used (LRU) page replacement policy do when physical memory is full and a new page must be brought in?
options: It evicts the page that has gone the LONGEST without being accessed, on the theory that recently-used pages are likely to be used again soon (temporal locality)
It evicts the most recently used page to make room for future access patterns
It evicts pages in the exact order they were originally loaded, regardless of usage
explanation: LRU approximates the idea that recently-accessed data is likely to be accessed again soon (temporal locality), so it targets the LEAST recently touched page for eviction as the one least likely to be needed again immediately. (Real implementations often use cheaper LRU approximations like the "clock"/second-chance algorithm rather than tracking exact access order.)

question: What is thrashing, in the context of virtual memory?
options: A state where the system spends most of its time paging data in and out of memory (because the combined working sets of running processes exceed available physical RAM) rather than doing useful work — throughput collapses even though the CPU appears "busy"
explanation: When physical memory is oversubscribed, processes constantly fault on pages that were just evicted to make room for something else, causing near-continuous disk I/O for paging instead of actual computation — a severe performance collapse called thrashing.

question: On a system call like `read()`, what typically happens to the calling thread while the kernel services the request from a slow device?
options: The thread keeps running instructions at full speed regardless

The thread is typically put into a blocked/sleeping state (removed from the scheduler's runnable queue) until the I/O completes, at which point it's marked runnable again — this is why blocking I/O in a latency-critical thread is problematic, since waking up incurs scheduling delay
The whole CPU halts entirely until the syscall returns
The kernel always converts the call into a busy-wait loop
explanation: Blocking I/O suspends the calling thread (freeing the CPU for other work) until the operation completes, then the scheduler must decide when to run it again — introducing scheduling latency and jitter, which is why hot paths in trading systems favor non-blocking/polling I/O or kernel-bypass techniques instead.

question: What is the average-case time complexity of quicksort, and what is its worst case?
options: Average O(n log n); worst O(n log n) as well — always the same
Average O(n log n); worst O(n^2) — e.g. when the pivot is always the smallest/largest element (already-sorted input with a naive pivot choice)
Average O(n^2); worst O(n log n)
explanation: Quicksort partitions around a pivot; with good pivot choices it splits roughly in half each time (O(n log n)), but a consistently bad pivot choice (e.g. always picking the first element on already-sorted data) degrades to O(n^2). Randomized or median-of-three pivot selection mitigates this in practice.

question: Which sorting algorithm is stable AND achieves O(n log n) worst-case time complexity?
explanation: Merge sort is both stable (equal elements retain their relative order) and O(n log n) in the worst case. Quicksort is typically not implemented stably and has O(n^2) worst case; heapsort is O(n log n) worst case but not stable; selection sort is O(n^2) and not stable.

question: What is the time complexity of binary search on a sorted array of n elements?
explanation: Binary search halves the remaining search space with each comparison, giving O(log n) time — but it REQUIRES the array to already be sorted and to support O(1) random access (which is why it works on arrays but not directly on a plain linked list).

question: What is the worst-case time complexity of searching for a key in an unbalanced binary search tree that has degenerated into a linked-list shape (e.g. from inserting already-sorted data)?
options: O(log n), same as a balanced tree
O(n) — the tree has effectively become a linked list
explanation: A BST's O(log n) guarantee assumes roughly balanced height. Inserting already-sorted keys into a naive (non-self-balancing) BST produces a degenerate, list-shaped tree of height n, making search O(n) — exactly why self-balancing trees (AVL, red-black) exist.

question: What is the time complexity of extracting the minimum element from a binary min-heap of n elements?
explanation: Removing the root (minimum) requires moving the last element to the root and "sifting it down" to restore the heap property, which takes O(log n) — the height of the heap. Peeking at the minimum without removing it, however, IS O(1).

question: Which data structure is most naturally suited to implementing an LRU (Least Recently Used) cache with O(1) get and put operations?
options: A hash map combined with a doubly linked list — the hash map gives O(1) lookup of a node, and the doubly linked list lets you move that node to the front (most-recently-used end) or evict from the back in O(1)
A plain array sorted by access time
explanation: The hash map provides O(1) key -> node lookup; the doubly linked list lets you unlink and re-link a node (moving it to the "most recently used" end) in O(1) without shifting other elements, and lets you evict the least-recently-used node (the list's tail) in O(1) as well.

question: What is the time complexity of the classic BFS (breadth-first search) traversal of a graph with V vertices and E edges?
explanation: BFS visits every vertex once and examines every edge once (in an adjacency-list representation), giving O(V + E) — this is the standard complexity for both BFS and DFS on a graph represented with adjacency lists.

question: Which algorithm is the standard choice for finding the shortest path in a graph with NON-NEGATIVE edge weights?
options: Kruskal's algorithm (that's for minimum spanning trees, not shortest path)
explanation: Dijkstra's algorithm, typically implemented with a priority queue (min-heap), finds shortest paths from a source vertex to all others in O((V+E) log V) — but it requires non-negative edge weights; graphs with negative weights need Bellman-Ford instead.

question: Why does Dijkstra's algorithm fail to produce correct results if the graph has negative edge weights?
options: It doesn't fail; it always works regardless of edge weights

Dijkstra greedily finalizes each vertex's shortest distance once popped from the priority queue, assuming no later-discovered (possibly negative-weight) path could ever improve on an already-finalized distance — a negative edge can violate that assumption, producing a wrong answer
Negative weights simply crash the algorithm
Dijkstra only works on undirected graphs
explanation: Dijkstra's greedy correctness proof relies on the invariant that once a vertex is finalized, no shorter path to it can be found later — which requires all edge weights to be non-negative. A negative edge discovered later could create a shorter path to an already-finalized vertex, which Dijkstra would miss. Bellman-Ford (O(V*E)) correctly handles negative weights (as long as there's no negative cycle).

question: What technique does dynamic programming rely on to improve exponential brute-force recursion (like naive Fibonacci) down to polynomial time?
options: Memoization/tabulation — caching (storing) the results of overlapping subproblems so they're computed once instead of recomputed exponentially many times
Reducing the precision of intermediate results
explanation: Naive recursive Fibonacci recomputes the same subproblems exponentially many times (fib(n-2) is computed separately by both the fib(n-1) and fib(n) branches, and so on). Memoization stores each subproblem's result the first time it's computed, turning an O(2^n) algorithm into O(n).

question: What is the space complexity of an in-place iterative reversal of a singly linked list?
explanation: An iterative in-place reversal only needs a fixed, constant number of pointer variables (prev, current, next) regardless of list length — O(1) extra space. A recursive reversal, by contrast, uses O(n) stack space due to the call stack.

question: What is the key property that makes the two-pointer technique applicable to a problem like "find two numbers in a SORTED array that sum to a target"?
options: The array must be unsorted for two-pointer to work

Because the array is sorted, moving the left pointer right always increases the current sum and moving the right pointer left always decreases it — giving a monotonic way to narrow toward the target in O(n) instead of checking all O(n^2) pairs
Two-pointer only works on linked lists, not arrays
It requires the array to contain only positive numbers
explanation: Sortedness gives monotonicity: starting pointers at both ends, if the current sum is too small you must move the left pointer right (to increase it), if too large move the right pointer left (to decrease it) — each pointer only moves in one direction, giving a linear O(n) scan instead of the brute-force O(n^2) pair check.

question: What is the purpose of the "sliding window" technique, typically applied to problems like "find the longest substring without repeating characters"?
options: It requires re-scanning the entire array for every window position, giving no improvement over brute force

It maintains a contiguous window (range) with pointers that expand/shrink incrementally, reusing previously computed information (e.g. a running count/set) instead of recomputing from scratch for every possible window — turning an O(n^2) or O(n^3) brute force into O(n)
It only applies to problems involving actual physical windows or UI elements
It requires sorting the input first
explanation: Instead of checking every possible substring/subarray from scratch (which is O(n^2) or worse), the sliding window incrementally adjusts a running window's boundaries and running state (e.g., a character-count map) as it slides, doing O(1) amortized work per step for an overall O(n) algorithm.

question: What is the time complexity of building a heap from an unsorted array of n elements using the standard bottom-up "heapify" approach (not inserting one element at a time)?
options: O(n) — a classic, non-obvious result: even though each individual sift-down is O(log n), most nodes are near the bottom (needing very few swaps), and the total work sums to O(n)
explanation: A common misconception is that building a heap costs O(n log n) (n sift-down operations, each O(log n)). The correct analysis accounts for the fact that most nodes are near the leaves and need very little sift-down work; summing the actual work across all levels gives a total of O(n), not O(n log n) — a classic "gotcha" interview question.

question: In a trie (prefix tree) storing n strings with total length L, what is the time complexity of checking whether a given string of length m is a stored prefix?
options: O(m) — independent of how many strings are stored, only dependent on the query string's own length
explanation: A trie lookup walks down one character at a time following child pointers matching each character of the query — its cost depends only on the LENGTH of the string being looked up (m), not on how many strings are stored in the trie, which is exactly why tries are attractive for prefix-matching / autocomplete-style problems over huge dictionaries.

question: Why is a hash map generally NOT a good choice for a problem that requires efficiently finding the SMALLEST key greater than or equal to X (a "successor" query)?
options: Hash maps cannot store numeric keys

A hash map provides O(1) average lookup for an EXACT key, but has no notion of ordering between keys — answering an ordered/range query like "successor of X" requires scanning, whereas an ordered structure like a balanced BST (e.g. std::map) supports it directly in O(log n) via its ordered traversal
Hash maps are always slower than arrays for every kind of query
Hash maps cannot be used with more than 1000 elements
explanation: Hashing deliberately discards ordering information to achieve O(1) average lookup for exact-match queries. Range/order-based queries (successor, predecessor, range sum) need a structure that maintains order, like a balanced BST (std::map's lower_bound/upper_bound) or a sorted array with binary search.

question: What is the amortized time complexity per operation of the union-find (disjoint-set) data structure, when using both union-by-rank/size AND path compression?
options: Nearly O(1) — technically O(α(n)), where α is the inverse Ackermann function, which grows so slowly it's effectively constant for any realistic input size
explanation: With both optimizations (union by rank/size to keep trees shallow, and path compression to flatten trees during find), the amortized cost per operation is O(α(n)) — the inverse Ackermann function, which is less than 5 for any n that could ever be represented in physical memory, so it's treated as effectively constant in practice.

question: What is the space complexity of the standard recursive merge sort implementation (including the auxiliary arrays used during merging)?
options: O(log n), only for the recursion stack
O(n), for the auxiliary arrays used during merging (plus O(log n) recursion stack)
explanation: Unlike quicksort, the standard merge sort implementation is NOT in-place — merging two sorted halves typically requires an auxiliary array of size O(n) to hold the merged result before copying it back, in addition to O(log n) recursion depth.

question: For a problem requiring you to repeatedly find and remove the maximum element from a dynamically changing collection (with insertions interleaved), which data structure gives the best asymptotic complexity for BOTH operations?
options: An unsorted array (O(1) insert, O(n) find-max)
A sorted array (O(n) insert, O(1) find-max)
A max-heap (O(log n) insert, O(log n) extract-max)
A hash set (O(1) insert, but no way to find max efficiently)
explanation: A binary max-heap gives O(log n) for both insertion and extract-max, a good balance for workloads needing both operations frequently — better overall than an unsorted array (fast insert, slow max) or a sorted array (fast max, slow insert) when both operations happen often.
